result:
There should be a small shop where you can buy back time you wasted.

Not years. Nothing grand enough to ruin the economy or tempt a king. Just the ordinary scraps: twelve minutes spent looking for your keys, an afternoon waiting for someone who never came, the half hour you stood in the kitchen scrolling through things you did not care about.

The shop would be narrow, between a locksmith and a bakery. Its hours would be inconvenient.

Behind the counter, a woman would ask, “What will you do with it?”

Most people would say something impressive. Learn Italian. Call their father. Watch the sunrise.

She would shake her head.

“You can’t spend it twice,” she’d explain. “If you’re already making it useful, you haven’t understood the merchandise.”

One day, you would arrive without an answer.

She would set a little paper envelope on the counter.

“Seven minutes,” she’d say. “From a meeting in April.”

“What does it cost?”

“Nothing. You were going to get those back eventually.”

Outside, the bakery would be closing. A boy in an apron would be sweeping flour from the threshold, carefully moving a beetle out of the broom’s path.

You would open the envelope.

Nothing would happen.

The light would stay on the buildings a little longer than seemed possible. You would sit on the low wall beside the bicycle rack. Somewhere nearby, a dog would make an unsuccessful argument.

For once, you would not reach for anything.

When the seven minutes were over, the boy would glance up from his sweeping.

“Nice evening,” he would say.

You would have to think about it.

“Yes,” you’d say. “It is.”
